definition: Two combined hip-posing defaults for an appealing weight-bearing stance: (1) weight is deliberately NOT split 50/50 between the legs — one leg is favored as the default, not an occasional choice — and (2) hip rotation is composed from all three axes at once (tilt, twist, AND bend together) rather than adjusting a single axis.
purpose: Make a weight-bearing pose read as organic and appealing rather than flat or robotic, using the hips as the single joint that carries most of a pose's sense of weight and intention.
visible_effect: The hips sit visibly higher on one side than the other (tilt), rotated toward the leg or direction taking the weight (twist), and leaning toward or away from camera (bend) — all three at once — rather than square, level, and facing forward.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: An evenly-split, single-axis hip pose reads as neutral-to-robotic; a favored leg combined with multi-axis hip rotation reads as a real person committing their weight somewhere, which is described as "far more appealing from a posing standpoint."
physical_interpretation: Real standing humans essentially never distribute weight perfectly evenly between both legs at once, and a hip free to tilt/twist/bend simultaneously (a ball-and-socket-adjacent joint region) is how the body actually redistributes weight and prepares to move.
use_cases: any standing or weight-bearing key pose, not only extreme action poses
a kicking, reaching, or off-balance action where the hips must clearly show which leg is carrying the weight
non_use_cases: a genuinely symmetric, evenly-balanced stance the design specifically calls for (e.g. a formal idle, a mechanical stance)
a style where hip posing is intentionally minimal or restrained
interactions: Hip rotation as the primary balance-correction lever (this batch, video 17) — that entry covers hip rotation CORRECTING for an already-extended limb's balance; this entry covers hip posing as a default APPEAL choice even before any limb extension is involved
Structural understanding — the existing card's balance/volume concern; this is a concrete, actionable pair of hip-posing defaults in service of that same concern

Asymmetry (`ai/vocabulary.js`, not implemented — "blocked_by: needs a mirror-aware pose editor") — this video is direct evidence for exactly that dimension: a deliberately uneven left/right weight split is named as the more appealing default, not an edge case
cadence_representation: The multi-axis half is fully representable today: hip rotation in Cadence is an ordinary joint rotation with three real rotational degrees of freedom, so tilt+twist+bend together is no different mechanically from rotating any other joint — nothing prevents composing all three right now via `set_keyframe`. The weight-asymmetry half is blocked exactly where the existing `asymmetry` dimension already says: `ai/vocabulary.js`'s `asymmetry` dimension is `implemented: false`, needing a mirror-aware pose editor this build does not have, so a caller cannot currently ask Cadence to "favor the left leg" as a declared intent — only pose each hip value directly and manually.
control_surface: Direct joint rotation (`set_keyframe`) can already combine all three hip axes; the `asymmetry` vocabulary dimension exists as a named concept for the weight-favoring half but compiles to nothing yet.
detection_and_measurement_methods: None dedicated — `ai/pose.js measurePose`'s balance/centre-of-mass measurement (against a declared support) could in principle confirm which leg is bearing more weight in a given pose, but nothing currently reads hip rotation values across all three axes and reports whether they are being used in combination versus on a single axis.
generation_or_modification_methods: Hip rotation across all three axes can already be authored directly through `authorMotion`'s pose-per-phase mechanism; nothing derives a "favor this leg" instruction into hip values automatically.
failure_modes: posing the hips level and square (an even 50/50 weight split) out of habit or caution, producing the flat, less appealing default this video argues against
adjusting only one hip rotation axis (commonly just twist) and leaving tilt and bend at rest, losing most of the appeal the combination produces
roblox_considerations: None specific — an ordinary joint-rotation concept applicable to any Roblox rig's hip/waist joint.
examples: Hector's ball-kick pose: the hips twist toward the kicking leg (taking the weight, letting the other leg stretch out), tilt to roughly a 45-degree angle, AND lean back away from camera, all at once — named directly as "using all these together creates better arcs, poses and weight" (video @ 3:54–4:23)

the general framing that a character's weight should never default to an even 50/50 split between legs, illustrated with Hector's and Miguel's own weight-shift moments in the soccer clip (video @ 2:59–3:32)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/fFf8EsPC_ws @ 2:59–4:23 — Rusty Animator states both defaults directly over paused and slow-motion clips from Pixar's *Coco*; frames in this session's sample confirm the surrounding scene setup (t=4:04, Hector and Miguel beside the soccer ball) but the specific multi-axis hip rotation itself plays between sampled frames rather than landing on one directly; experimental until validated
